Their coherence is substantive and pair-specific: both require learners to compose their own original written text at BASIC 3, in complementary genres of the same Writing strand (informative recount of observed/pictured events versus a short argumentative paragraph), so classroom work on one genuinely reinforces composition capability exercised in the other. This is not dependency: the target's defining demand (formulating an opinion/claim and supplying clear reasons) is absent from the source indicator, the two sit in different sub-strands taught in parallel within the same grade, and the source's own code ordering places Sub-Strand 13 before Sub-Strand 14, so no developmental sequence is evidenced; the generic sentence-to-paragraph complexity argument is not sufficient substantive same-rank evidence for buildsTowards. Shared Strand/Grade ancestors, the single shared LC tag 'writing', the shared token 'write' (jaccard ~0.06), the weak 'b3' code prefix and same-page (117) proximity were treated as nomination signals only, never as semantic verdicts. Limitations: 24 source-evidence items are omitted per endpoint and the second endpoint's source_refs excerpt is truncated, and all endpoints/ancestors carry upstream audit/merge context (including the merged BASIC 3 grade organizer), which is retained rather than resolved; these limits reduce but do not remove confidence in the symmetric reading.

That is substantive, pair-specific instructional coherence rather than mere repeated wording, so relatesTo is warranted. A same-rank buildsTowards is not supported: the two indicators are co-listed parallel expectations in the same source table row, and the only directional signals available are weak or non-semantic (sequential code order .3 then .4, 'level-appropriate texts' token/trigram overlap, page proximity, shared ancestors, shared LC tags 'reading'/'comprehension'). No evidence shows that independent reading deepens, extends, or combines the visualisation strategy specifically, and the generic claim that a comprehension strategy aids independent reading would apply to every indicator in this sub-strand. Confidence is moderated because the pair's nomination evidence and both endpoints' source/LC evidence are truncated, and all endpoint ancestors carry upstream audit/merge context (including merged Strand and Grade organizers) that has been preserved rather than resolved.

Source evidence and one LC record for the second SFI are truncated, but the retained statement text and hierarchy are sufficient for this symmetric judgment.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 2 (rank 1) Indicators under the same Reading / Phonics Content Standard B2.2.2.1 ('Connect sounds to letters and blend letters/syllables in order to read and write'), so direction rests on statement substance rather than rank. B2.2.2.1.1 is the narrow generative skill of blending syllables to produce words (LC tags: blending, phonics, syllables, words). B2.2.2.1.2 applies alphabetic knowledge to decode unknown words across a substantially broader set of units - beginning/ending consonants, consonant blends, consonant digraphs, vowel sounds, vowel digraphs and word patterns - evidenced by its six distinct decoding LCs. Reliable syllable blending is the sound-combining operation that supports success at decoding unfamiliar words using these varied letter-sound patterns, so the first indicator builds towards the second; the reverse is not supported because decoding unknown words presupposes rather than enables basic blending.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 3 Indicators under Strand 2: Reading (rank 2 for both), but in different sub-strands: 'Use consonant blends to build words' (B3.2.5.1.1, Sub-Strand 5: Blends and Consonant Clusters, under standard 'Identify and use consonant blends in words') and 'Use basic elements of structural analysis (e.g prefixes, suffixes, compound, root words) to decode unknown words' (B3.2.2.1.3, Sub-Strand 2: Phonics, under 'Connect sounds to letters and blend letters/syllables in order to read and write'). They are coherent, complementary word-level skills: one manipulates sound-level consonant clusters to construct words, the other analyses morphological units to decode unfamiliar words, and both LCs share the 'phonics' tag. The evidence shows no substantive deepening or extension of one into the other at the same grade rank — the units of analysis (phonemes/blends vs. morphemes) differ rather than nest — so a same-rank developmental direction is not warranted; meaningful reinforcement within Basic 3 word-recognition work supports relatesTo. Shared Strand/Grade ancestry, weak code-prefix overlap ('b3','2'), and page proximity alone were not treated as semantic evidence, and the generic token overlap ('to','use','words') was discounted. Noted limitations: source evidence for both endpoints and the second endpoint's LC metadata are truncated, so the full exemplar text is not available.

Endpoint source and LC evidence are truncated, limiting deeper verification but not the coherent word-reading link.

Shared Strand/Grade ancestry, the b3.2 code prefix, page-104 proximity, and 'use/build/words' token overlap were not treated as sufficient. judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 1 (rank 0) Indicators under the same Content Standard B1.5.1.1 'Apply knowledge of capitalisation in writing' (Strand 5 Using Writing Conventions/Grammar Usage, Sub-Strand 1 Using Capitalisation), so the grain and topic match. Same-rank direction is supported by pair-specific text, not merely by code order: B1.5.1.1.2 targets capitalising a bounded, concrete set — titles and names of people (LCs 'Use capital letters at the beginning of names of people', 'Capitalise titles of texts') — while B1.5.1.1.3 explicitly says 'other proper nouns' (LC tagged 'proper nouns'; source context cites writing names of towns and particular places), a formulation that presupposes the people/title cases and broadens the skill to the general proper-noun category. Control of capitalisation for familiar personal names/titles therefore supports success in generalising capitalisation to other proper nouns, giving buildsTowards from the second UUID (B1.5.1.1.2) to the first (B1.5.1.1.3). Evidence limits: nomination evidence and both endpoints' source/LC excerpts are truncated, and ancestors carry merge/continuation audit context (B1.5.1.1 row-1/row-2 CONT'D merge), though the two indicator texts themselves are untruncated and sufficient.

Accordingly this is symmetric relatesTo with null direction. judgment.rationale: B2.2.2.1.2 (BASIC 2, Strand 2: Reading / Sub-Strand 2: Phonics, under 'Connect sounds to letters and blend letters/syllables in order to read and write') asks learners to use alphabetic knowledge — beginning/ending consonants, blends, digraphs, vowel sounds, vowel digraphs and word patterns — to decode unknown words; its Learning Components are all decoding skills. B2.2.9.1.3 (BASIC 2, Strand 2: Reading / Sub-Strand 9: Fluency, under 'Read texts fluently') asks learners to use contextual clues to confirm or self-correct pronunciation while reading aloud; its single Learning Component mirrors that wording (tags: contextual clues, pronunciation, reading aloud, self-correct). The two are substantively coherent as complementary strategies for arriving at and checking correct word pronunciation in reading — phonics-based decoding alongside context-based confirmation and self-correction — so this is more than generic repetition or shared Reading-strand wording. However, they share the same Grade coordinate BASIC 2 (rank 1), and the evidence does not substantiate a same-rank developmental claim: the fluency indicator does not deepen or extend the phonics capability but recruits a different (semantic/contextual) cue system in a parallel sub-strand, and the nomination signals are only shared Strand/Grade ancestors, a weak 'b2'/'2' code prefix, and trivial token overlap ('use', 'to', 'reading'). relatesTo with null direction is therefore the correct symmetric judgment. Limitations: both endpoints omit 24 source-evidence items and carry upstream audit/merge context (merged B2.2.2.1 CONT'D standard, merged BASIC 2 grade heading), so the full source wording is unavailable and the assessment rests on the supplied statement text, hierarchy and Learning Components.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 1 Indicators (same statement-type grain, same coordinate rank 0), so direction rests on substantive content rather than rank. B1.4.3.1.2 (Strand 4 Writing, Sub-Strand 3 'Writing Letters – Small and Capital', under standard 'Use general skills strategies and knowledge of letter sounds to write legibly and boldly') asks pupils to copy names of objects correctly in both upper and lower case letters — i.e. accurate formation and discrimination of capital versus small letter forms while writing names. B1.5.1.1.2 (Strand 5 Using Writing Convention/Grammar Usage, Sub-Strand 1 'Using Capitalisation', under 'Apply knowledge of capitalisation in writing') asks pupils to use capital letters at the beginning of titles and names of people; its LCs are 'Capitalise titles of texts' and 'Use capital letters at the beginning of names of people'. Reliably producing correct upper- and lower-case forms when writing names is an enabling motor/orthographic skill that supports the later rule-governed choice of capitalising names and titles, so proficiency in the first raises likelihood of success in the second. The overlap is not merely lexical ('letters', 'names'): the first supplies letter-case production, the second adds a convention-based application, a substantive extension rather than repetition. Evidence limits: both endpoints' source evidence excerpts are truncated (24 omitted source-evidence items each) and the second endpoint's LC evidence is truncated, and grade organiser/content-standard ancestors carry upstream merge context, so the judgment rests on the bounded statement text, Strand/Sub-Strand placement and LCs supplied.

Both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each) and all endpoints and ancestors carry upstream audit/merge context, including a merged BASIC 3 grade organizer and a merged parent Content Standard B3.1.6.1; this limits but does not contradict the symmetric reading.

judgment.rationale: Both indicators sit at BASIC 1 (rank 0), so direction rests on substantive content, not coordinate order. B1.2.2.1.4 (Reading / Sub-Strand 2: Phonics, under 'Connect sounds to letters and blend letters/syllables in order to read and write') requires blending sounds into simple syllables/words and syllables into words; its LCs are 'Blend sounds to produce simple syllables/words' and 'Blend syllables to produce words'. B1.5.10.1.1 (Using Writing Conventions / Sub-Strand 10: Spelling) requires identifying and spelling simple words correctly, and its parent Content Standard is explicitly 'Use phonics knowledge to spell words' with LC tags including 'phonics'. Sound/syllable blending proficiency is the phonics capability the spelling indicator draws on to encode simple words, so success in the blending indicator supports success in the spelling indicator (second_to_first). This is a pair-specific phonics-to-spelling link, not mere shared 'simple words' wording or a shared BASIC 1 grade parent. Evidence is bounded: source evidence for both SFIs and LC metadata for the second endpoint are truncated, so omitted exemplars could not be inspected.

judgment.rationale: Both endpoints are Indicators at the same grain and the same resolved Grade coordinate (BASIC 3, rank 2, gap 0), sharing Strand 4: Writing and Sub-Strand 9: Writing as a Process but placed under different Content Standards. The second SFI (B3.4.9.1.1, under B3.4.9.1 'Apply the skills and strategies for idea generation, selection, development, organization and revision in writing') covers pre-writing planning: selecting a familiar topic, brainstorming and organising ideas (LCs 'Select a topic on familiar themes e.g. Myself', 'Brainstorm ideas before writing', 'Organise ideas before writing'). The first SFI (B3.4.9.3.3, under B3.4.9.3 'Apply strategies for improving drafts for publishing') is an oral publishing/presentation act: reading one's own writing aloud to a group or whole class (LC tags: own writing, presentation, read aloud). These are complementary, mutually reinforcing phases of a single writing-process sub-strand taught in the same grade, which is substantive instructional coherence beyond the weak nomination signals (token jaccard 0.07-0.09 driven by 'a'/'writing', weak b3.4.9 code prefix, same-rank proximity). However, the evidence does not establish a developmental dependency in either direction: proficiency in topic selection, brainstorming and organising ideas is not shown to raise the likelihood of success at the distinct oral presentation skill of reading aloud to an audience, and same-rank buildsTowards requires substantive pair-specific evidence that is absent here. Symmetric relatesTo with null direction is therefore the correct judgment, with canonical endpoint order retained. Evidence limitation: 24 source-evidence items are omitted for each endpoint and the second endpoint's source-ref excerpt is truncated, so only bounded statement text, Content Standard parents and Learning Components were used; all endpoints carry upstream audit/merge/code context (including the merged BASIC 3 grade organizer) that was inspected but not silently resolved.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 1 (rank 0) Indicators under STRAND 4: WRITING, so the grain and coordinate match and same-rank direction must rest on substantive content. B1.4.7.1.1 (Sub-Strand 7, Controlled Writing; parent standard 'Write simple compositions') requires finding, reading and copying whole sentences from a substitution table, i.e. the same copying skill applied at sentence level and combined with locating and reading within a controlled table. Accurate legible copying of words/letters plausibly supports success in copying correct sentences toward simple composition, so the developmental direction runs from the letter/word-level indicator to the sentence-level controlled-writing indicator. The shared 'copy' token alone would be weak, but the LC evidence ('Copy the names of objects correctly in both upper and lower case letters' vs 'Copy sentences from a given substitution table', plus find/read components) shows genuine skill extension rather than generic repetition. Confidence is moderated because both endpoints' source evidence is truncated and the endpoints sit in different sub-strands at the same grade, so no teaching sequence is asserted.

They cohere substantively around early encoding of words in writing (accurate spelling of simple words vs. approximate/invented spelling in self-directed writing), which is meaningful complementary reinforcement across strands. Shared parent-grade, weak token/trigram overlap ('simple', 'spelling' tag) and code prefix 'b1' alone were not treated as semantic evidence. The shared object is the same ('ideas ... in sentences', reflected in both sets of LCs), and the grammar indicator extends composing ideas in simple sentences to combining those ideas into compound sentences via coordinating conjunctions — the sub-strand title itself names the simple-to-compound sequence. Facility with writing ideas in simple sentences therefore supports success in joining ideas with coordinating conjunctions, not the reverse; this is expanded capability rather than repeated wording. Evidence limitation: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted source-evidence items each), so the judgment rests on the statement text, sub-strand/strand context, and LCs supplied.

However, neither statement extends or deepens the other in a way that makes one's proficiency a support for the other: one processes meaning from a heard/read text, the other applies character understanding to real-life connection within storytelling, and same-rank placement supplies no directional evidence. This is meaningful complementary reinforcement, warranting a symmetric relatesTo rather than a developmental direction. Endpoint source evidence and some LC metadata are truncated, but the retained statement text and hierarchy are sufficient for this judgment.

judgment.rationale: Both endpoints sit at BASIC 3 (rank 2), so direction rests on substantive content, not rank. The second SFI (B3.2.2.1.1, Reading / Phonics) asks learners to 'Understand the relationship between spelling of words and sounds of speech', under the parent Content Standard 'Connect sounds to letters and blend letters/syllables in order to read and write' — an explicit link from phonic sound-letter knowledge to writing. The first SFI (B3.4.9.3.2, Writing / Writing as a Process) requires learners to 'Proofread draft to correct punctuation and spelling errors', with a supplied Learning Component 'Proofread draft to correct spelling errors'. Grasping grapheme–phoneme/spelling–sound correspondences plausibly supports the likelihood of success in detecting and correcting misspellings while proofreading one's own draft, so the phonics indicator builds towards the proofreading indicator. The shared evidence is not mere repeated wording: the token overlap ('spelling') is backed by a substantive skill link from decoding/encoding knowledge to applied spelling correction. Note the first indicator also covers punctuation, which the phonics indicator does not support, limiting the scope of the dependency; confidence is moderate accordingly. Source-evidence truncation on both endpoints and LC truncation on the second SFI mean some supporting exemplar text is unavailable.

B3.3.13.1.1 (Sub-Strand 13: Persuasive/Argumentative Writing, under 'Support an opinion in writing') requires composing a short paragraph supporting an opinion or claim with clear reasons, and its bounded source-context label shows the exemplar 'Choose a simple topic for an argument', i.e. the same topic-selection/idea-organisation moves applied to an argumentative product. Proficiency in generating, selecting and organising ideas before writing plausibly supports success in producing an organised, reason-supported opinion paragraph; the reverse is not supported. The shared 'writing' tag and Strand/Grade ancestry alone were not treated as sufficient; the pair-specific prewriting-to-composition link is the basis. Confidence is moderate because the link is an enabling process skill applied to a genre task rather than an explicit curricular sequence, and both endpoints' source evidence excerpts are truncated.

The pair-specific developmental change is substantive rather than mere wording overlap on 'describe': command of descriptive qualifying words at the short-sentence level is the linguistic resource that is then deployed at extended discourse level to produce a coherent descriptive paragraph about places. The supplied Learning Components confirm this (identify adjectives / use adjectives in short sentences to describe vs. describe places in a coherent paragraph), so sentence-level adjective proficiency plausibly supports success in paragraph-level description; the reverse is not supported. Same-rank direction is therefore justified by evidence of increased linguistic scope and complexity, not by rank or code prefix, which are only weak nomination signals. Evidence limitation: source evidence for both endpoints is truncated and both carry upstream audit/merge context, so this is an inferred curriculum-grounded relation at moderate confidence.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 1 Indicators (same statement-type grain, coordinate rank 0) under STRAND 2: READING. judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 2 Indicators (same statement-type grain, identical coordinate rank 1), so any developmental direction would need substantive same-rank evidence. B2.1.7.1.4 sits under Strand 1 Oral Language / Sub-Strand 7 Listening Comprehension (Content Standard B2.1.7.1, 'Use appropriate skills and strategies to process meaning from texts') and asks learners to share facts from texts heard; B2.2.7.2.3 sits under Strand 2 Reading / Sub-Strand 7 Comprehension (Content Standard B2.2.7.2, 'Use knowledge skills and techniques of reading to understand and interpret texts') and asks learners to connect characters, ideas and information within a text. Both LCs carry the 'comprehension' tag, and the two indicators are complementary text-meaning work across the listening and reading modalities: recalling and orally reporting factual content versus relating story elements and ideas internally to a text. The evidence shows conceptual coherence in text comprehension but no indication that proficiency in one is needed for or specifically supports the other (different strands, different processing demands, shared grade), so a symmetric relatesTo is the supported judgment rather than a directional buildsTowards. Lexical overlap is negligible ('a', trigram fragments) and the shared BASIC 2 ancestor and 'b2' code prefix alone were not treated as semantic evidence. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated, so this rests on the bounded statement text, hierarchy and LC tags supplied.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 1 Indicators (same grade rank 0), so no rank-based developmental direction applies, and neither statement shows substantive expansion of the other. Evidence is mainly thin token overlap ('stories') plus a shared grade ancestor, which alone would not suffice; the pair-specific narrative-understanding coherence supports symmetric relatesTo only. judgment.rationale: Both are Basic 3 Indicators (same statement-type grain, same Grade rank 2) under Strand 2: Reading, but in different sub-strands: B3.2.2.1.2 (Phonics) asks learners to use alphabetic knowledge to decode unknown words (blends, digraphs, vowel sounds, word patterns), while B3.2.6.1.1 (Vocabulary) asks learners to read level-appropriate sight words and understand and use them in meaningful complex sentences. These are complementary word-recognition/word-meaning skills that reinforce each other in reading: decoding handles unfamiliar words, sight-word reading handles automatically recognized words and extends to meaning and sentence use. The evidence shows no substantive expansion of one skill into the other, and at equal rank there is no source-backed basis for asserting that proficiency in either specifically supports success in the other, so a symmetric conceptual relation is the supported judgment rather than a developmental direction. Shared tokens ('words', 'use') and the weak shared code prefix (b3, 2) alone were not treated as progression evidence. Endpoint source evidence and one LC record are truncated, but the visible statement texts are sufficient for this symmetric judgment.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 1 Indicators (same grade rank 0, same statement-type grain). First (B1.2.2.1.2, Strand 2 Reading / Sub-Strand Phonics) is oral-visual letter knowledge: 'Recognise and produce letter names and sounds randomly'. Second (B1.4.3.1.2, Strand 4 Writing / Sub-Strand Writing Letters – Small and Capital) is a transcription task: 'Copy the names of objects correctly in both upper and lower case letters'. They cohere substantively around alphabetic letter knowledge across reading and writing — the second's parent Content Standard B1.4.3.1 explicitly invokes 'knowledge of letter sounds to write legibly' — but the copying indicator is a visual-motor upper/lower-case reproduction task that does not evidentially depend on random letter-name/sound production, and at equal rank there is no substantive evidence establishing a developmental direction. The lexical overlap flagged in nomination ('names', 'and') is partly spurious ('letter names' vs 'names of objects'), so complementary reinforcement rather than buildsTowards is the supported reading.

Their Learning Components confirm the divergence (coordinating conjunctions/grammar/joining ideas vs select topic/brainstorm/organise ideas). No source evidence links sentence-level conjunction use to the planning stage of the writing process, and neither text nor LC set indicates that proficiency in one supports success in the other or constitutes meaningful pair-specific reinforcement. Endpoint source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each), so absence of a link in this bounded excerpt is not proof of absence, but the available evidence supports neither a developmental nor a substantive coherence claim.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 2 Indicators (same statement-type grain, same resolved coordinate rank 1, so no lower-to-higher direction is available from the grade sequence). However, the supplied evidence shows parallel same-grade treatment in two different strands rather than a documented expansion of capability from one to the other; recognising/discussing versus describing story events is complementary reinforcement, not an evidenced dependency, so symmetric relatesTo is the supported judgment rather than a same-rank buildsTowards. Both endpoints carry upstream audit/merge context and truncated source evidence, which limits but does not contradict this reading.

Direction at equal grade rank is supported by the recognition-to-production shift and the second indicator's revision framing, not merely by the shared token 'letters' or shared 'b1' code prefix, which alone would be insufficient. judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 1 Reading Indicators (same grade rank 0), so direction rests on substantive content, not coordinate gap. The second SFI (B1.2.1.2.3, Sub-Strand 1 Pre-Reading Activities, under Content Standard 'Manipulate the sounds of the letters of English') is oral phonemic-awareness work: its Learning Components are saying the new word after phoneme deletion, addition of an initial sound, and substitution of initial/middle/final sounds. The first SFI (B1.2.2.1.3, Sub-Strand 2 Phonics, under 'Connect sounds to letters and blend letters/syllables in order to read and write') asks learners to understand the relationship between the spelling of words and the sounds of speech, i.e. mapping phonemes onto graphemes. Facility in isolating and manipulating individual speech sounds in spoken words is the oral capability that makes the spelling-to-sound correspondence tractable, so proficiency in the second supports success in the first; the reverse dependence is not supported, since the phoneme-manipulation indicator is explicitly oral/pre-reading and requires no orthographic knowledge. Shared 'sounds' LC tag and code prefix alone were not treated as evidence. Note that both endpoints' source evidence is truncated and several ancestors carry merge/CONT'D extraction context, which limits but does not contradict this reading.

judgment.rationale: Both are Indicator-grain statements in STRAND 4: WRITING at the same coordinate (BASIC 1, rank 0), so direction rests on substantive evidence rather than rank. The second SFI (B1.4.5.1.3, Sub-Strand 5 'Writing Simple Words and Sentences', parent Content Standard B1.4.5.1 'Write words and sentences') targets sentence-level production—using basic descriptive words to write a simple sentence. The first SFI (B1.4.7.1.3, Sub-Strand 7 'Controlled Writing', parent Content Standard B1.4.7.1 'Write simple compositions') moves beyond single sentences to matching sentence parts so as to compose meaningful connected texts. Competence in constructing and enriching individual sentences plausibly supports success at assembling sentence parts into coherent composition-level texts, a broadening from sentence to text unit within the same strand; the within-grade sub-strand and code ordering (B1.4.5 before B1.4.7) is consistent with, though not by itself decisive for, this direction. Both endpoints carry upstream audit/merge context and truncated source evidence, so the excerpts seen are bounded and the judgment is inferred curriculum coherence, not empirical prerequisite proof.

Pre-writing muscular-control activity plausibly supports success in clear letter copying, so a same-rank developmental direction from pre-writing to penmanship is substantively supported by the sub-strand content rather than by code prefix, page proximity, or the trivial shared token 'of'. Evidence limits: both endpoints' source evidence excerpts are truncated (24 omitted items each) and all nodes carry upstream audit/merge context, so the judgment rests on the bounded statement, sub-strand, content-standard and LC text shown.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 3 Indicators (rank 2, same grade coordinate) under Strand 5 'Using Writing Conventions/Grammar Usage', but in different Sub-Strands and under different Content Standards: B3.5.4.1.3 (Sub-Strand 4 'Using Action Words'; parent B3.5.4.1 'Apply knowledge of action words in communication') requires using simple past and past continuous verb forms to express past actions, while B3.5.5.1.1 (Sub-Strand 5 'Using Qualifying Words - Adjectives'; parent B3.5.5.1 'Apply knowledge of adjectives in communication') requires identifying and using adjectives in short sentences to describe height, length, etc. Their Learning Components confirm distinct content (past continuous/simple past verb forms vs identifying and using adjectives), so neither is evidence of dependency on or preparation for the other; the shared strand, grade rank gap of 0, weak code prefix ('b3','5'), adjacent pages 120/121, and token overlap limited to 'and/to/use' cannot establish direction. However, they are substantively coherent complementary grammar-usage skills: each applies knowledge of a specific word class within sentence-level written/spoken communication under the same strand's 'apply knowledge of X in communication' construction, which supports a symmetric relatesTo rather than mere generic repetition. producer_judgment.rationale: Both endpoints are BASIC 3 Indicators (rank 2, identical canonical grade coordinate) within Strand 1: Oral Language, but under different Sub-Strands and different Content Standards: B3.1.9.1.1 'Give and respond to commands, instructions and directions' (Sub-Strand 9, giving/responding to commands) and B3.1.8.1.2 'Use appropriate pronunciation and intonation in asking and answering the inversion questions' (Sub-Strand 8, asking/answering questions). Their Learning Components confirm complementary rather than dependent skills: producing and responding to directives versus prosodic control (pronunciation/intonation) when initiating and answering inversion questions. Both train the same underlying oral initiate-and-respond exchange pattern, so they cohere substantively and reinforce each other, but neither statement's evidence shows that proficiency in one conditions success in the other, and equal rank with distinct sub-strand content gives no substantive basis for a same-rank developmental direction. The nomination signals (shared Strand/Grade ancestors, code prefix 'b3.1', adjacent source pages 98-99, and token/trigram overlap limited to 'and') are structural and weak, so only the symmetric relation is supported. Source evidence for both SFIs is truncated (24 omitted evidence items each), which bounds but does not contradict this reading.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 1 Indicators (same grain, same rank 0), so direction rests on substantive content rather than coordinate order. Reliable production of upper- vs lower-case letter forms when writing names plausibly supports success at applying the capitalisation convention to proper nouns; the second extends handwriting/case-form control into rule-governed convention use. This is inferred curriculum coherence, not an asserted mandatory prerequisite; the shared token 'letters' and shared BASIC 1 grade ancestor alone were not treated as sufficient. judgment.rationale: Both endpoints are BASIC 2 Indicators (same grain, both coordinates resolved at rank 1). B2.4.5.1.3 (Strand 4: Writing / Sub-Strand 5: Writing Simple Words and Sentences) requires drawing a picture and writing at least a sentence to share an opinion; its parent Content Standard B2.4.5.1 frames this as using knowledge of grammar and vocabulary to write words and sentences correctly. B2.5.4.1.1 (Strand 5: Using Writing Conventions/Grammar Usage / Sub-Strand 4: Using Action Words, under B2.5.4.1 'Apply knowledge of action words in communication') requires using the simple present tense to express habitual actions, including simple truths, interest, feelings and opinions. There is real, pair-specific coherence: one indicator supplies a grammatical means of expressing opinions and the other requires an opinion expressed in a written sentence, so they reinforce each other as complementary grammar and composition work within the same grade. The evidence does not, however, support a developmental claim at equal rank: the writing indicator prescribes no tense or grammatical structure, the parent standard refers to grammar only generically rather than to the simple present, and 'opinions' appears in the grammar indicator only as one item in a parenthetical list of meanings. Nomination signals (shared Grade ancestor, 0.08 token / 0.13 trigram jaccard dominated by 'and'/'to', rank_gap 0 'weak', 'b2' code prefix 'weak') were treated as routing hints, not semantic evidence. Symmetric relatesTo with null direction therefore fits; confidence is moderated because source evidence and supporting LC evidence are truncated for both endpoints (24 omitted source evidence items each) and both endpoints and all ancestors carry upstream audit/merge/code context, including the merged BASIC 2 grade organizer and the merged, continuation-page B2.4.5.1 content standard.

judgment.rationale: Both Indicators sit in BASIC 2 (rank 1), Strand 4: Writing, so grain and statement type match. B2.4.5.1.3 (Sub-Strand 5: Writing Simple Words and Sentences, under 'Use knowledge of grammar and vocabulary to write words and sentences correctly') asks learners to draw a picture and write at least one sentence to share an opinion — its LCs are 'draw pictures to share an opinion' and 'write at least a sentence to share an opinion', i.e. picture-supported, sentence-level composition. B2.4.10.1.1 (Sub-Strand 10: Narrative Writing, under 'Narrate situations, express feelings and convey point of view about the real or fictional world') asks learners to write about real or imagined experiences or events using the process approach — extended, multi-stage text composition about real/fictional events. Within the same grade, reliable sentence-level opinion writing plausibly supports success in composing longer narrative pieces through the process approach, so the substantive expansion (single supported sentence to staged extended narrative) justifies a same-rank developmental direction from the second SFI to the first rather than mere shared 'write' wording or shared Strand/Grade ancestry. Evidence limits: both endpoints' source evidence excerpts are truncated (24 omitted source evidence items each) and the second endpoint's supporting LC metadata is truncated, and several ancestors carry upstream merge/audit context (BASIC 2 grade heading merged as case duplicate; B2.4.5.1 merged as a CONT'D continuation), which does not alter the statement texts used here but tempers confidence.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 3 Indicators (rank 2, gap 0) in Strand 1: Oral Language but under different Sub-Strands: B3.1.9.1.1 'Give and respond to commands, instructions and directions' (Sub-Strand 9) and B3.1.8.1.1 'Ask and answer questions for clarifications about given topics' (Sub-Strand 8). Their Learning Components (give/respond to commands, directions; ask/answer questions for clarification) show substantive coherence as complementary two-way oral interaction skills: producing an utterance and responding appropriately to a partner's utterance within spoken discourse, so each meaningfully reinforces the other's listening-and-speaking exchange behaviours. However, the evidence shows no substantive dependency: neither commanding nor questioning is presented as a precondition for the other, they sit in parallel sub-strands under separate Content Standards, and same-rank placement with only weak nomination signals (shared 'and', code prefix 'b3.1', adjacent pages 98/99) cannot establish developmental direction. Symmetric relatesTo is therefore the supported judgment. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated and both carry upstream audit/merge context, which limits but does not contradict this reading.

judgment.rationale: Both are Content Standards in BASIC 3 (rank 2), Strand 4: Writing, so grain and grade scope match. Direction at equal rank rests on this letter-to-word/sentence capability expansion, not on shared Strand, adjacent codes, page proximity, or generic shared tokens ('write', 'knowledge', 'and', 'of'), which alone would not justify an edge. Evidence limitation: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 and 35 omitted source evidence items), no Learning Components are supplied, and the second endpoint is an upstream merge of a CONT'D occurrence with slightly differing wording, so the judgment rests on the bounded statement text and hierarchy only.

judgment.rationale: Both endpoints are BASIC 3 Indicators (same statement-type grain, both resolved at Grade rank 2). Same-rank buildsTowards requires substantive evidence that is not present, so the symmetric relatesTo with null direction and preserved canonical endpoint order is the complete judgment. judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 1 Content Standards (same grain, same coordinate rank 0) centred on the letters of the English alphabet, but they sit in different strands with different capability foci: B1.2.1.2 (Strand 2 Reading / Sub-Strand 1 Pre-Reading Activities) is phonological — manipulating the sounds of letters — while B1.4.2.1 (Strand 4 Writing / Sub-Strand 2 Penmanship) is graphomotor — copying and writing letter forms correctly. This is substantive complementary coherence in early alphabet/letter knowledge across reading and writing, reinforcing the same letter set from sound and form sides, but the evidence shows no dependency: correct letter formation does not require sound manipulation, and sound manipulation does not require handwriting proficiency. With equal rank and no source evidence of a taught order or expanded capability, a same-rank developmental direction is unsupported, so the symmetric relation is correct. Both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (34 and 24 omitted items) and both carry upstream merge/audit context (B1.2.1.2 merged from a duplicated CONT'D row), which limits but does not contradict this reading.

judgment.rationale: Both are Content Standards at the same BASIC 3 rank in Strand 4: Writing, so grain and coordinate permit a same-rank judgment, but the sub-strand evidence shows a foundational-to-applied relationship rather than mere repetition. B3.4.5.1 (Sub-Strand 5: Writing Simple Words and Sentences) requires learners to 'Write accurately using acquired vocabulary and knowledge of grammar' — sentence-level accuracy, word choice and grammatical control. B3.4.14.1 (Sub-Strand 14: Informative/Academic Writing) requires learners to 'Write on the events of the day', an extended informative composition task whose source row shows it realised through writing picture events 'using simple sentences'. Control of accurate vocabulary and grammar in simple sentences plausibly supports success in composing informative accounts of daily events, so the supported direction is second_to_first. Shared strand/grade and the weak 'write'/'of' token overlap alone were not treated as sufficient; the substantive basis is the sentence-accuracy-to-composition relation. Evidence is bounded: both endpoints have truncated source evidence (24 and 35 omitted items) and no Learning Components were supplied, and B3.4.5.1 is an upstream-merged continuation record whose two source renderings differ slightly in wording ('acquired vocabulary' vs 'word recognition and knowledge of grammar and vocabulary'), which limits but does not contradict this reading.

judgment.rationale: Both endpoints are BASIC 2 Content Standards (same statement-type grain; resolved Grade coordinate rank 1 for each, gap 0), so developmental direction cannot come from rank and must be earned from text. B2.2.2.1 (Strand 2 Reading / Sub-Strand 2 Phonics) is 'Connect sounds to letters and blend letters/syllables in order to read and write'; B2.4.10.1 (Strand 4 Writing / Sub-Strand 10 Narrative Writing) is 'Narrate situations, express feelings and convey point of view about the real or fictional world'. The phonics standard's own stated purpose includes writing, and the narrative standard is written composition at the same grade, giving substantive complementary coherence between encoding skill and composing connected text — useful instructional coherence rather than mere shared wording. However, the two statements share no capability that one visibly extends: one is sound–letter/blending mechanics, the other is communicative purpose and point of view, with no transcription or phonics language in the target. The 'phonics enables writing' inference is generic across all writing standards and is not pair-specific enough to support a same-rank buildsTowards claim, so the symmetric relatesTo judgment is taken with canonical endpoint order preserved and null direction. Nomination signals (shared BASIC 2 Grade ancestor at distance 3/3, weak 'b2' code-prefix, token jaccard 0.04 on 'and', trigram fragments 'con'/'rea'/'s a') are structural/lexical only and were disregarded as semantic evidence. Evidence limits: no Learning Components supplied for either endpoint; source evidence truncated for both (35 and 24 omitted items) with one source-ref excerpt itself truncated; upstream merge context applies to the BASIC 2 grade organizer and to B2.2.2.1 (CONT'D row merge), and those anomalies remain unresolved here.

judgment.rationale: Both endpoints are Indicator-grain statements in Strand 2: Reading, Sub-Strand 7: Comprehension (B2.2.7.2.1 at BASIC 2, rank 1; B3.2.7.2.4 at BASIC 3, rank 2), so the grain and topical coherence conditions are met and the permitted developmental direction would be second_to_first. However, the pair-specific content differs in kind rather than in depth: the BASIC 2 indicator targets metatextual knowledge of the purpose and features of information texts (LC tags: comprehension, purpose, features, information texts), while the BASIC 3 indicator targets independent reading of level-appropriate texts (LC tags: comprehension, independent, reading). Independent reading rests principally on decoding, fluency and level-matching rather than on text-type feature awareness, so the evidence does not support asserting that proficiency in the BASIC 2 indicator materially raises likelihood of success in the BASIC 3 indicator; the shared signal is the reusable 'comprehension' tag and the token 'texts' (low Jaccard 0.08-0.14), which is generic overlap. Meaningful reinforcement within the same Reading/Comprehension sub-strand across grades supports symmetric relatesTo instead. Ancestor and endpoint audit/merge context and truncated source evidence were considered and do not alter this reading.

judgment.rationale: Both endpoints are Indicators in Strand 2: Reading within the same framework, so grain matches. The second SFI (B1.2.1.2.2, BASIC 1, rank 0, under 'Manipulate the sounds of the letters of English' / Pre-Reading Activities) requires orally segmenting spoken syllables/words into individual sounds; the first SFI (B2.2.2.1.1, BASIC 2, rank 1, under 'Connect sounds to letters and blend letters/syllables in order to read and write' / Phonics) requires blending syllables to produce words. Shared LC tags and text ('phonics', 'syllables', 'sounds', 'words') confirm a common phonological/phonemic skill base rather than mere wording repetition: oral awareness and control of syllable/sound units at BASIC 1 plausibly supports the later capability of blending syllables into whole words within decoding at BASIC 2, an expansion from oral analysis to synthesis for reading/writing. Direction lower-to-higher rank (second_to_first) is the only permitted developmental direction and matches this evidence. Endpoint source evidence and LC metadata are truncated, so the judgment rests on the bounded excerpts and codes shown.

judgment.rationale: First (B3.4.2.1.1, BASIC 3, Strand 4 Writing / Sub-Strand 2 Penmanship-Handwriting) is 'Copy short paragraphs clearly' — a handwriting legibility/transcription indicator under the standard 'Copy and write sentences correctly'. Second (B2.4.8.1.1, BASIC 2, Strand 4 Writing / Sub-Strand 8 Guided Composition) is 'Develop two coherent paragraphs on one idea or concept using leading questions' — a composition/idea-generation indicator under 'Compose short paragraphs through answering questions'. judgment.rationale: Same statement-type grain (both Indicators). B1.2.1.1.1 'Handle books appropriately' (BASIC 1, rank 0; Strand 2: Reading, Sub-Strand 1: Pre-Reading Activities, under B1.2.1.1 'Know how a text works for reading and writing') is an emergent print-concepts/book-handling behaviour. B2.6.1.1.1 'Read a variety of age and level-appropriate books and texts from print and non-print' (BASIC 2, rank 1; Strand 6: Extensive Reading, Sub-Strand 1: Building the Love and Culture of Reading, under B2.6.1.1 'Read widely for pleasure and to demonstrate independent reading and learning in the literary area') is about sustained independent engagement with varied texts. The two are substantively coherent and mutually reinforcing within early reading instruction: knowing how to handle and orient to books complements building a habit of reading varied print and non-print materials, so this is more than generic repetition of the token 'books'. But the evidence shows no substantive extension, deepening, or combination of the BASIC 1 capability in the BASIC 2 indicator — wide independent reading depends on decoding, fluency and comprehension capabilities that are not evidenced as growth from book handling, and the endpoints sit in different strands and sub-strands. Symmetric relatesTo with null direction is therefore the supported judgment.
